name: De Stijl / Neoplasticism
origin: Theo van Doesburg founded the journal 'De Stijl' in Leiden in 1917 and with it the movement of the same name; its core included Piet Mondrian, Vilmos Huszár, the architect J.J.P. Oud and the furniture maker Gerrit Rietveld. After the experience of the First World War they sought a universal harmony freed from any individual hand – Mondrian called the program 'Nieuwe Beelding', neoplasticisme. The means was radical reduction: horizontals and verticals only, the three primary colors plus black, white and gray only, no curve, no diagonal, no representation. The movement effectively ended with van Doesburg's death in 1931; its grammar traveled through the Bauhaus into modern design as a whole.
idea: The layout itself is the picture: rectangles of unequal size, separated by black bars of varying weight, balanced without symmetry.
markers: Horizontals and verticals only – 0 diagonals, 0 curves, radius 0px
Black separating bars in graduated weights: 4px / 6px / 10px / 18px within one composition
Red #D22B1F, blue #1F3D99 and yellow #F2C40B only, as fills on off-white #F5F3EE
Color under 25% of the surface, white remains the dominant field
Asymmetric balance: nothing centered, no field the same size as another
Color fields sit at edges and corners, never in the middle
No shadows, no gradients, no transparency – flat fills only
Blocky grotesque, set in caps, weights 700-900
Buttons and fields are not objects on a surface but cells of the composition

params.depth: none; order comes exclusively from the weight of the black bars
params.color: Off-white as the ground field, plus exactly three primary colors as solid rectangles and black as structure.
params.type: Blocky grotesque in caps, heavy weights, negative tracking – the type is one surface among others.
params.motion: Strictly orthogonal: color changes in 120ms linear, translation along X or Y only, never scaling or rotation.

examples.name: Piet Mondrian, 'Composition with Red, Blue and Yellow' (1930)
examples.what: One dominant red field at the top right, tiny blue and yellow fields below, black bars in clearly different weights – the canonical study in balance

examples.name: Gerrit Rietveld, Rood-blauwe stoel (1918/1923)
examples.what: The style in three dimensions: interpenetrating black slats, seat and back in red and blue, every component staying visible as its own plane

examples.name: Theo van Doesburg, covers of the journal 'De Stijl' (from 1917)
examples.what: Purely rectilinear letter construction, the title set as a grid of bars – typography as architecture

examples.name: Rietveld Schröder House, Utrecht (1924)
examples.what: A facade of freely shifted planes with colored lines; proof that the composition itself is the ordering principle, not the decoration

examples.name: Bento grid layouts (2023-2026, including Apple product pages)
examples.what: The structural descendant: tiles of unequal size, clearly separated, individual ones accented in color – De Stijl with radius and shadow

strengths: The layout is the brand – recognition without a logo, an illustration or a font license
Bento grids are the direct modern heir and are excellent for feature overviews, dashboards and home screens
Purely flat and therefore pixel-exact on every platform, with no GPU cost
Forces a real hierarchy decision: which cell is large, which one is colored – arbitrariness is structurally ruled out
risks: Decorative and functionally thin as a full style: the composition has to be rebuilt per screen and survives no dynamic content
Too few hierarchy levels for dense applications – the system breaks at the fourth level
Uneven bar weights quickly turn it into a Mondrian quotation rather than a language of your own; the association is overpowering
Yellow is unusable as a text field; colored cells may carry only black or white
Responsive work is expensive: an asymmetric composition cannot simply reflow, it has to be recomposed per breakpoint
a11y: The color fields themselves are uncritical as long as the text on them is controlled: off-white on red #D22B1F lands at 4.6:1, on blue #1F3D99 at 8.7:1, black on yellow #F2C40B at 11.4:1 – white on yellow, by contrast, at 1.5:1, which is forbidden. The red is therefore only just compliant and carries body text only, no 10px labels. Thick black bars are accessibility-neutral and even help delineate blocks. The real risk is structural: once buttons are nothing but colored cells of the composition, the affordance is missing – so focus rings have to be set 4px thick and inset in a contrasting color, and the DOM order has to follow the visual reading order, because grid areas easily pull the two apart.
longevity: The grammar is over a hundred years old and still works unchanged, but it is so tightly linked to Mondrian that every application reads as a quotation. In the bento variant it visibly carries the 2023-2025 timestamp.

platforms.web: Very good – CSS Grid with named areas is the exact technical equivalent, including bars of different weight via border plus gap.
platforms.mobile: Weak – the asymmetric composition collapses into a stack on narrow displays and loses exactly the distinguishing feature.
platforms.desktop: Good for overview and home screens in Tauri, unsuitable for dense lists, tables and settings dialogs.

verdict: As a continuous product language no, as a signature layout a yes worth considering. The temptation is strong for a solo developer, because De Stijl looks instantly unmistakable with pure CSS Grid and not a single asset – but that unmistakability belongs to Mondrian rather than to your own brand, and across 27 apps it quickly feels like a costume. On top of that comes the practical break: a hand-composed asymmetric surface tolerates no dynamic lists, no settings dialogs and no Android screen. The style makes sense as a recurring special surface – home screen, launcher, app overview, marketing hero – over a quiet Swiss grid for the actual UI.
tip: Grade the black bars deliberately in at least three different weights and let no two fields end up the same size. A bento grid with an even gap and equally sized tiles is not De Stijl, it is a grid – the whole style lives on the eye resolving the inequality into equilibrium. And keep color under a quarter of the surface: white is the main color, not the leftover.
